column1: What is Angular, according to its own documentation?
column2: A TypeScript-based, component-based application PLATFORM for building UIs — not just a rendering library. It ships with its own conventions for components, templates/binding, module organization, dependency injection, routing, and HTTP.

column1: What core problem does Angular's declarative data binding solve?
column2: In vanilla JS you must manually re-run DOM-update code every time data changes (e.g. element.textContent = ...), and it's easy to forget a spot. Angular lets you describe the desired UI state declaratively, and it automatically keeps the DOM in sync when data changes.

column1: What three things make up every Angular component?
column2: 1) A class (TypeScript) holding data and logic. 2) A template (HTML with Angular syntax) describing what to render. 3) Styles scoped to that component.

column1: Is AngularJS the same framework as modern Angular?
column2: No. AngularJS (1.x) used JavaScript, controllers, and $scope-based two-way binding. Modern Angular (2+) is a rewrite using TypeScript and a component-tree architecture designed for better performance and scalability.

column1: What command creates a brand-new Angular project?
column2: `ng new my-app` — scaffolds the full file/folder structure, installs dependencies, and sets up TypeScript/build configuration.

column1: What does `ng serve` do?
column2: Starts a local dev server (default http://localhost:4200) and watches your files, automatically rebuilding and refreshing the browser whenever you save a change (live reload).

column1: What command generates a new component, and what does it create?
column2: `ng generate component <name>` (short: `ng g component <name>`). It creates a folder with the component's class file (.ts), template (.html), stylesheet (.css), and a spec/test file, and automatically makes it usable elsewhere.

column1: In current Angular (v17+), do new components need to be registered in an NgModule?
column2: No — current Angular defaults to standalone components, which are directly importable without any NgModule `declarations` registration. Older Angular versions required manual NgModule registration.

column1: What Angular building block is described as 'instructions attached to DOM elements/templates that change behavior or appearance'?
column2: Directives (e.g. `*ngIf`, `*ngFor`, `ngClass`).

column1: What does `{{ value }}` (interpolation) do, and in which direction does data flow?
column2: Inserts the current value of a class property into the template as text. Data flows one-way: Class → Template.

column1: What does `[property]="value"` (property binding) do, and in which direction does data flow?
column2: Binds a component's data to an actual DOM element property (not just text) — e.g. `src`, `disabled`. Data flows one-way: Class → Template, and it passes the real evaluated value (boolean, number, object), not just a string.

column1: What does `(event)="handler()"` (event binding) do, and in which direction does data flow?
column2: Runs a component method in response to a DOM event like click or input. Data flows Template → Class (user interaction back into your component logic).

column1: What does `[(ngModel)]="value"` (two-way binding) do, and what must be imported to use it?
column2: Combines property binding and event binding so data flows both ways at once (typically with form inputs). Requires `FormsModule` to be imported/added to the component's `imports: []` — unlike interpolation/property/event binding, it isn't available by default.

column1: Why does `<button disabled="{{ isAvailable }}">` NOT correctly disable/enable the button?
column2: Interpolation inside an attribute produces a plain string, and in HTML the mere PRESENCE of the `disabled` attribute (any value, even 'false') disables the button. You need property binding `[disabled]="!isAvailable"` so the actual boolean value is passed to the DOM property.

column1: What is `[(ngModel)]` literally shorthand for?
column2: `[ngModel]="dessertName" (ngModelChange)="dessertName = $event"` — property binding sets the value, event binding updates it on change ('banana in a box').

column1: What special variable does Angular provide inside an event binding to access the native DOM event?
column2: `$event` — e.g. `(input)="onInput($event)"`.

column1: What are the two categories of Angular directives beyond components, and what does each change?
column2: Structural directives (e.g. `*ngIf`, `*ngFor`) add/remove entire elements from the DOM, marked with a leading `*`. Attribute directives (e.g. `ngClass`, `ngStyle`) change the look/behavior of an element that already exists in the DOM, no leading `*`.

column1: What actually happens to an element and its child components when `*ngIf`'s condition becomes false?
column2: Angular DESTROYS the element (and any component inside it) entirely, running cleanup — it does not just visually hide it like CSS `display: none`. If the condition becomes true again, it's recreated fresh, so any internal state resets.

column1: What does `*ngFor="let dessert of desserts; let i = index"` give you access to?
column2: `dessert` — the current item in the loop, and `i` — the zero-based index/position of that item.

column1: What is `trackBy` used for with `*ngFor`?
column2: A performance optimization: a function (e.g. `trackByDessertId`) that returns a unique identifier per item, so Angular can efficiently track which DOM elements correspond to which data items across re-renders.

column1: Why can't you put `*ngIf` and `*ngFor` on the same element?
column2: Angular doesn't allow two structural directives on one element (ambiguous order of operations). Instead wrap them across separate elements, e.g. put `*ngFor` on an `<ng-container>` and `*ngIf` on the element inside it.

column1: How does `[ngClass]="{ 'sold-out': !dessert.available }"` work?
column2: Takes an object where each key is a CSS class name and each value is a boolean expression; the class is applied when its condition is true and removed when false.

column1: When should you prefer `[class.sold-out]="condition"` over `[ngClass]="{...}"`?
column2: When you only need to toggle a single class based on a single condition — it's simpler and arguably clearer than `ngClass`, which is better suited to multiple classes toggled by multiple independent conditions.

column1: When should you use `ngStyle` instead of `ngClass`?
column2: Only when the value itself is dynamic/computed and can't reasonably be expressed as a fixed set of predefined CSS classes (e.g. a percentage-based width). Prefer `ngClass`/`[class.x]` otherwise, since predefined classes keep style in your CSS files and benefit from the cascade.

column1: What problem does `@Input`/`@Output` communication solve?
column2: It gives components a defined way to talk to each other: a parent passes data DOWN to a child (`@Input`), and a child notifies the parent of events UP (`@Output` + `EventEmitter`) — without it, split-up components would have no clean way to communicate.

column1: How does a parent pass data to a child component using `@Input`?
column2: The child marks a property with `@Input()` (e.g. `@Input() dessert!: {...}`); the parent uses ordinary property-binding syntax on the child's custom tag, e.g. `<app-dessert-card [dessert]="d">`.

column1: How does a child component notify its parent of an event using `@Output`?
column2: The child declares `@Output() selected = new EventEmitter<T>();` and calls `this.selected.emit(value)` to fire it. The parent listens with ordinary event-binding syntax: `(selected)="onDessertSelected($event)"`, where `$event` is whatever was passed to `.emit()`.

column1: Why does an `@Input()` property often need a `!` (non-null assertion) in TypeScript?
column2: Angular sets `@Input()` values AFTER the class is constructed, not in the constructor, so at compile time the property isn't guaranteed to have a value yet. The `!` tells TypeScript 'trust me, this will be set before use.'

column1: What is `ngOnInit`, and when does Angular call it?
column2: A lifecycle method Angular calls automatically once, right after a component's `@Input()` properties have been set for the first time — a natural place for initial setup logic.

column1: Why shouldn't you read an `@Input()` value inside a component's constructor?
column2: The constructor runs BEFORE Angular has finished setting `@Input()` properties from the parent, so reading it there can give `undefined`. `ngOnInit` runs after inputs are set, making it the safe place for input-dependent setup.
